books.title: Not the End of the World
books.why: Data-driven tour of emissions, energy, food and pollution by Our World in Data's lead researcher. Best antidote to doom.

books.title: How to Avoid a Climate Disaster
books.why: Frames everything around 51 billion tons of CO2e and the 'green premium' - the cost gap between clean and dirty options.

books.title: Speed & Scale
books.why: An action plan with OKRs for each sector. Useful for thinking like an operator about what moves the needle.

books.title: How the World Really Works
books.why: Why cement, steel, plastics and ammonia make decarbonization hard. Makes you fluent in energy orders of magnitude.

books.title: Electrify
books.why: The case for electrifying everything at home - heat pumps, EVs, induction, rooftop solar - with the math.

books.title: The New Map
books.why: Geopolitics of oil, gas and the transition. Explains why energy prices swing with wars, OPEC and LNG.

books.title: The Price Is Wrong
books.why: Cheap solar isn't enough - it's profitability and financing that drive buildout. Key for understanding PPAs and power markets.

books.title: Short Circuiting Policy
books.why: How utilities and interest groups shape clean energy laws state by state.

books.title: The Grid
books.why: Readable history of the US power grid and why integrating renewables is a wiring problem as much as a generation problem.

books.title: Abundance
books.why: Why permitting and process slow clean energy and transmission - a big theme in today's energy news.

books.title: Sustainable Energy - Without the Hot Air
books.why: Free online classic. Teaches you to do back-of-envelope kWh/day math for any energy claim.

books.title: Drawdown
books.why: Ranks 100 climate solutions by impact. Pair with drawdown.org's updated data.

books.title: Doughnut Economics
books.why: The framework behind a lot of 'sustainable development' thinking: meeting human needs within planetary boundaries.

books.title: Saving Us
books.why: How to talk about climate with anyone - useful if you're the 'pro' in the room.

books.title: The Ministry for the Future
books.why: Novel about the next decades of climate policy, carbon coins and geoengineering. Widely read in the industry.

glossary.def: kW is power (rate); kWh is energy (amount). A 1 kW heater running for 3 hours uses 3 kWh. Your bill charges per kWh.
Actual output divided by maximum possible output over a year. US solar is roughly 20-25%, onshore wind 30-40%, nuclear above 90%.
Levelized cost of energy: lifetime cost per MWh of a power plant. New utility solar and onshore wind are among the cheapest sources before subsidies.
Power purchase agreement: a long-term contract to buy electricity from a project at a set price. How corporations buy renewable power.
Power plants are dispatched cheapest-first; the last (most expensive) plant needed sets the wholesale price. This is why gas prices drive electricity prices.
Midday solar floods the grid, pushing net demand and prices down (sometimes negative), then demand ramps up at sunset. Batteries shift that solar into the evening.
Grid operators (e.g. PJM) pay plants to be available in future years. Recent PJM auctions cleared at record prices as data-center demand grew.
The waiting line to connect new plants to the grid - often years long and a major bottleneck for renewables.
Scope 1: direct emissions you burn. Scope 2: purchased electricity and heat. Scope 3: everything in your value chain - usually the largest share.
Carbon-dioxide equivalent converts all greenhouse gases using global warming potential. Methane is about 28-30x CO2 over 100 years and over 80x over 20 years.
Net zero (per SBTi) means cutting about 90% of emissions and removing the rest. 'Carbon neutral' claims often rely on buying offsets.
Avoidance offsets pay to prevent emissions elsewhere; removals (forests, direct air capture, enhanced weathering) pull CO2 out. Removals are higher-quality and pricier.
Renewable energy certificates: 1 REC = 1 MWh of renewable generation. Unbundled RECs are a weak claim; additional PPAs are stronger.
Coefficient of performance: units of heat delivered per unit of electricity. Modern heat pumps reach 2.5-4, meaning 250-400% efficient versus about 95% for a gas furnace.
Energy used per unit of GDP (or per square foot or per product). Falling intensity is how efficiency shows up in the data.
The July 2025 budget law phases down wind and solar credits: projects must begin construction by July 4, 2026, or be in service by end of 2027. Storage, nuclear and geothermal credits last longer.
The UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals (2015-2030). SDG 7 is clean, affordable energy; SDG 13 is climate action.
